title: Sariputta's lion's roar
hookLine: accused of a slight, Sariputta says he is like the earth that bears all things without complaint (AN 9.11)
carry: a mind like the earth, without ill will

cards: He hit me, and he left without a word of apology. That's the complaint, more or less. The rainy season is over at Savatthi, and Sariputta has just said goodbye to the Buddha and set out on the road.
Behind him, a monk goes to the Buddha and says Sariputta struck him and walked off. The Buddha doesn't settle it himself. He sends for Sariputta.
And word goes around the monastery that something worth hearing is about to happen. In the Anguttara Nikaya, this is Sariputta's lion's roar.

teach.b: First, what he doesn't say. Sariputta doesn't call the man a liar or list his own good deeds. He begins, in paraphrase: someone who wasn't mindful of the body might strike a fellow monk and walk away without apologizing.
Then he describes his own mind with a picture. Second, the earth. People throw all kinds of things on the earth, he says, clean things and filthy things.
And the earth isn't repelled, isn't ashamed, isn't disgusted. It just bears it. In the same way, he says, I live with a mind like the earth: wide, large, without hostility and without ill will.
Third, more pictures. Water washes clean things and filthy things without turning away. Wind blows over all of it.
A dusting cloth wipes up whatever it's given. Each image shows the same thing from another side: a mind that takes what comes without striking back. Fourth, the ending, and the surprising part.
The monk who made the accusation falls at the Buddha's feet and admits he spoke falsely.
The Buddha tells Sariputta to pardon him. And Sariputta says, in paraphrase: I pardon him, if he asks me to. And let him pardon me too.
The one who was wronged asks to be forgiven as well.
The Dhammapada uses the same picture for someone who has done the work: patient like the earth. Not a doormat, in this story. Sariputta speaks, clearly, in front of everyone.
He just doesn't throw anything back.

how: Monks and nuns in some Buddhist communities ask one another's forgiveness at set times, and Sariputta's earth image is taught as a model of patience under criticism.

o: feeling grounded by walking barefoot outside
bearing what's thrown at you without ill will
staying silent and never defending yourself

games.q: Sariputta's lion's roar: tap the pairs.
p: says he was struck, with no apology
bears clean and filthy things alike

s: Sariputta called his accuser a liar
he never attacked the man; he described his own mind as being like the earth.
the accuser admitted in the end that he had spoken falsely
he fell at the Buddha's feet and confessed.
he pardoned him, and asked to be pardoned too.

games.q: you're Sariputta. a fellow monk has told the Buddha you struck him and left without apologizing, and now you've been called back in front of everyone. what do you do?
o: deny it and demand an apology.
describe a mind that is like the earth.
say nothing and go back to the road.
games.why: he speaks of the earth, water, wind and a dusting cloth: a mind without ill will. the accuser confesses, and Sariputta pardons him and asks to be pardoned too.

practice: Feel your weight resting on the seat, the floor, the ground beneath the building, and let that ground be the picture.
Bring up one small slight from the last few days, let it land the way things land on the earth, and notice the urge to throw something back, leaving it unthrown.

wordCard.voice: Like the earth. Accused before the Buddha, Sariputta says his mind is like the earth, which bears clean and filthy things alike without ill will. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the earth, the first of Sariputta's images for a mind without ill will.

carryVoice: Your line: a mind like the earth, without ill will. Clean or filthy, the earth just bears it, and throws nothing back. Day seven hundred thirty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 9.11, Sihanada Sutta (Sariputta's lion's roar)
